paper.title: Making Reliable Distributed Systems in the Presence of Software Errors
paper.venue: Doctoral dissertation, Royal Institute of Technology

read_sources.note: Read for thesis statement, telecom requirements, error-isolation philosophy, let-it-crash rule, supervisor hierarchies, OTP behaviours, and AXD301 case evidence.

summary.one_sentence: Armstrong's thesis argues that reliable systems can be built from faulty software by isolating concurrent processes, letting failed workers crash, and delegating recovery to explicit supervision hierarchies.
summary.thesis: The core claim is not that errors disappear; it is that runtime architecture must assume errors, contain them, detect them, and restart the smallest safe unit of work.
summary.why_it_matters: Modern agents are long-running programs made of model calls, tools, memory updates, and side effects. Armstrong gives the older systems vocabulary for making that shape survivable: isolation boundaries, restart specifications, supervisors, degraded service, and protocol-level fault detection.

prior_state: Large telecom systems had to run continuously despite shipping with software defects.
Traditional defensive programming mixed business logic and error recovery in the same code path.
Distributed programs needed to tolerate process, message, software, and hardware failures without stopping the entire system.
Reliability requirements were operational, not cosmetic: phone switches were expected to provide acceptable service over years of continuous operation.
problem.key_gap: The thesis asks how to program systems that behave reasonably even when the components implementing them contain software errors.
assumptions: Large systems will contain software errors after deployment.
Fault isolation is more realistic than proving all application code correct.
Processes can be isolated and connected through message passing.
A runtime can detect process exits and restart workers or dependent groups.
Some degraded service is better than whole-system failure.

concepts.name: Fault isolation
concepts.definition: The runtime property that a software error in one process should not corrupt or directly crash unrelated work.

concepts.name: Let it crash
concepts.definition: The coding rule that when a worker encounters an error it cannot handle, it should fail and let a supervising process perform recovery.

concepts.name: Supervisor
concepts.definition: A process responsible for monitoring workers or other supervisors and starting, stopping, or restarting them according to a specification.

concepts.name: Supervision tree
concepts.definition: A hierarchy of supervisors and workers that encodes restart relationships and failure domains.

concepts.name: AND/OR supervision
concepts.definition: A distinction between dependent groups that restart together and independent children where only the failed child restarts.

concepts.name: OTP behaviour
concepts.definition: A reusable Erlang/OTP pattern such as gen_server, gen_event, gen_fsm, supervisor, or application that separates generic runtime structure from application logic.

method.core_idea: Organize the system as isolated tasks with explicit goals; when a task cannot achieve its goal, abort that task and delegate recovery to a supervisor that knows how to restart the right process or subtree.
action_grammar: worker: a process that performs application work.
supervisor: a process that watches workers or lower supervisors.
exit signal: runtime notification that a process failed or stopped.
restart specification: data describing how to start, stop, or restart a child.
OR supervision: restart only the failed independent child.
AND supervision: restart a dependent group when one child fails.
restart frequency: limit beyond which the supervisor itself fails upward.
steps: Partition the application into isolated processes that communicate by message passing.
Define the goals and acceptable degraded modes of the system as a task hierarchy.
Write workers so that unrecoverable local errors crash instead of tangling business logic with generic recovery.
Attach workers and lower supervisors to supervision trees with start/stop/restart specifications.
Use OR supervision for independent workers and AND supervision for dependent process groups.
Escalate failure upward when a subtree restarts too often or cannot reestablish a good state.
Use reusable OTP behaviours so runtime mechanics are not reimplemented in every application module.

claims.statement: The thesis treats software errors as expected in large deployed systems and designs for acceptable behavior despite them.
caveats: The empirical setting is telecom systems, not LLM agents.

claims.statement: Fault isolation is the central runtime requirement: errors in one task must not propagate arbitrarily to unrelated tasks.
caveats: The thesis relies on Erlang's process model; other runtimes must recreate equivalent boundaries explicitly.

claims.statement: The let-it-crash rule separates application work from generic recovery by letting workers fail and supervisors repair the system.
caveats: Crash-and-restart is safe only when state, side effects, and idempotency are handled by the runtime design.

claims.statement: Supervisors encode restart policy in a hierarchy and can restart one child, a dependent group, or fail upward when restart limits are exceeded.
caveats: Restart policy is not automatic correctness; bad restart specifications can recreate the same failure.

claims.statement: OTP behaviours package generic runtime structure so application modules do not each implement servers, event handlers, finite-state machines, and supervisors from scratch.
caveats: The thesis focuses on Erlang/OTP and does not prescribe direct API designs for modern workflow engines.

claims.statement: The AXD301 case study reports a large deployed OTP system with a supervision tree of 141 nodes and 191 behaviour instances.
caveats: This is case-study evidence, not a controlled comparison against other reliability architectures.

evidence.result: Armstrong states that large programs will probably contain errors when put into service and asks how to build systems that behave reasonably despite those errors.
The thesis identifies fault isolation as the essential problem: isolate code for each goal so errors can be detected and prevented from propagating to other simultaneous goals.
The thesis explicitly says workers should crash on errors they cannot handle, while separate supervisor processes are responsible for correction and recovery.

Supervisors monitor workers or other supervisors, keep start/stop/restart specifications, restart failed children under OR supervision, restart groups under AND supervision, and can fail upward after exceeding restart frequency limits.
The thesis presents primitive behaviours such as client-server, event handling, and FSM behaviours, then uses supervisor behaviours to compose them into supervision hierarchies.
In the AXD301 analysis, the thesis reports a supervision tree with 141 nodes and 191 OTP behaviour instances, including gen_server, gen_event, supervisor, gen_fsm, and application behaviours.

agent_infra_takeaways: A serious agent runtime needs a supervision tree, even if it calls it a workflow, retry policy, task graph, or orchestration plan.
Letting an agent step fail is only safe when the runtime knows what state to discard, what state to replay, and which side effects are already committed.
Agent workers should be small failure domains: model call, tool call, parser, verifier, memory update, and finalizer are different restart units.
Generic recovery belongs in the runtime layer; task-specific reasoning belongs in the worker.
Restart budgets matter. Infinite retry loops are not supervision; they are unbounded failure amplification.
Capability-style process names in Armstrong's model rhyme with modern tool permissions: if a worker cannot name or reach a resource, it cannot affect it.
caveats: The thesis predates cloud workflow engines, containers, LLMs, and modern exactly-once execution patterns.
Crash-only recovery can duplicate external side effects unless the runtime records and deduplicates them.
Erlang process isolation is stronger and more uniform than many agent frameworks' in-process task abstractions.
The telecom case studies prove practical viability in that domain, not universal superiority for every distributed architecture.
Supervision handles failure recovery; it does not by itself solve prompt injection, authorization, or semantic task correctness.

related_work.title: Durable Execution
related_work.note: Durable execution adds persisted step results to the restart-oriented reliability story, making replay safe across process and machine crashes.

related_work.title: DBOS
related_work.note: DBOS pushes the runtime state that supervisors need into database tables and transactions.

related_work.title: ReAct
related_work.note: A ReAct loop needs supervision because each thought-action-observation step can fail, block, duplicate, or corrupt state.

poc.note: No PoC yet - contributions welcome. A minimal PoC could model an agent task as workers under a supervisor with bounded restart counts and idempotent step logs.
